rationale: A wins because it keeps the story inside the facts and finds three clean protagonists: user, founder, investor. Its best headline, "The app that made women message first will now help write the message," is a real tension; B's "Dating apps add AI to write your opening line - and some users hate it" tries to sell a category trend on one company's relaunch. That's not fatal, but it is the kind of padding that gets a founder into trouble with a reporter who asks for the second example.
gaps_in_A: "The relaunch is the founder's first big public move since returning as CEO this year" is not in the supplied facts. It may be true, but it needs confirmation before it becomes the why-now.

"The market is pricing it before any post-relaunch paying-user data exists" overstates the evidence. The facts say the stock fell and the metric is not yet reported; they do not give current market reaction to the relaunch.
"Bumble's entire brand is a single authentic human gesture" is sharp, but a little grand for the fact block. The safer version is the women-message-first model remains core.
gaps_in_B: "Dating apps add AI to write your opening line" is a plural trend claim with one company as evidence. The set even admits Bumble is "one example, not the proof of a movement"; that should have killed or narrowed the angle.

"the Dorsey/Schultz/Kalanick-adjacent storyline" imports a flashy founder-return archetype that is not needed and not grounded in the update. It makes the clean founder angle smell like pundit shorthand.

The broad authenticity angle and the women-first contrarian angle are too close without outside proof: "who are you actually talking to?" and "Does AI-assisted messaging strengthen or hollow out the women-first principle?" are adjacent versions of the same AI-authenticity friction.
"four distinct shapes exist" overclaims. There are three strong shapes here; the fourth is a trend wrapper that needs external reporting before it earns a slot.
